```{r}
library(MetaboCoreUtils)
library(xcms)
library(MsExperiment)
library(MetaboAnnotation)
library(Spectra)
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)
```

## Introduction

The objective of this demo is to perform compound annotation based on an in-house database, created with the information gathered from the injection of a series of authentic standards with the same analytical protocol used for the samples.
For that we will use the file from "mix 2", which contains the following compounds:

- Malvidin-3,5-diglucoside, C29H35O17+
- Quercitrin-3-rhamnoside, C21H20O11
- Laricitrin, C16H12O8
- Quercetin-3-galactoside, C21H20O12
- o-Coumaric acid, C9H8O3
- Gallic acid, C7H6O5
- Procyanidin B3, C30H26O12
- Procyanidin A2, C30H24O12


## Create the in-house library

The first step is to create our library with the information of the standards.
For that, we create a reference database with the m/z values of the [M-H]^-^ ion, which is the most common ion we see with our analytical setup.

```{r}
stds_tb <- data.frame(
  name = c("Malvidin-3,5-diglucoside", "Quercitrin-3-rhamnoside", "Laricitrin",
           "Quercetin-3-galactoside", "o-Coumaric acid", "Gallic acid",
           "Procyanidin B3", "Procyanidin A2"),
  formula = c("C29H34O17", "C21H20O11", "C16H12O8", "C21H20O12",
              "C9H8O3", "C7H6O5", "C30H26O12", "C30H24O12")
)
```

To calculate masses and m/z values we use the functions of the package [`MetaboCoreUtils`](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/MetaboCoreUtils.html):

```{r}
stds_tb$mass <- calculateMass(stds_tb$formula)
stds_tb$mz <- as.numeric(mass2mz(stds_tb$mass, "[M-H]-"))
stds_tb
```

Here we have the table with the theoretical m/z values that we expect to find in the injection of the standards.

The next step is to determine their retention times. For that, we do chromatographic peak detection in the file of the injection of the standards.

```{r}
## import the file
std_files <- list.files("../data/wines/", pattern = "mix02", full.names = TRUE)
std_raw <- readMsExperiment(spectraFiles = std_files) |>
  filterMsLevel(1)   ## only full scan

## peak picking
cwp <- CentWaveParam(peakwidth = c(5, 30),    ## expected range of chromatographic peak width
                     ppm = 5,                 ## tolerance to identify ROIs in the mz/rt plane
                     prefilter = c(5, 50000), ## at least 5 consecutive scans with a signal higher than 50000
                     noise = 5000)
register(SerialParam()) ## setting xcms in serial mode
std_cw <- findChromPeaks(std_raw, param = cwp)

std_pks <- chromPeaks(std_cw)
std_pks[1:20, ]
```

In total `r nrow(std_pks)` chromatographic peaks have been identified. This is much more than what we would expect, since the sample is a mixture of `r nrow(stds_tb)` pure standards ... Do you have any idea that could explain why the number of peaks is so much larger than the number of compounds in this sample?


We now annotate these chromatographic peaks using only their m/z values.
For that we use the functions of the package [`MetaboAnnotation`](https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/MetaboAnnotation.html).
To annotate the detected peaks we use the function `matchMz()` against the reference database we have just created:

```{r}
pks_match <- matchMz(
  std_pks, stds_tb, param = MzParam(ppm = 10)
)
pks_match
```

The result object handles the potential many-to-many matching between chromatographic peaks (*query*) and reference compounds (*target*), and contains all the information of both the query and the target objects, together with the score of the match (in this case the difference between the m/z values).
For example, here we can see that `r length(unique(na.omit(matchedData(pks_match)$target_name)))` of the `r nrow(stds_tb)` reference compounds were found among the detected chromatographic peaks.
We can extract the full matching table with the function `matchedData()`. This returns a table with all the queries (i.e., chromatographic peaks) in the rows and the corresponding matches in the columns whose names start with "target_". If a query (i.e., chromatographic peak) matches more than one element of the target (i.e., reference database), its row is duplicated in the returned table. For the rows that cannot be matched NA values are reported.

```{r}
tb_match <- matchedData(pks_match)
tb_match
```

Not all chromatographic peaks were annotated, while in other cases more than one chromatographic peak was assigned to the same compound.
Let's keep only the annotated chromatographic peaks:

```{r}
tb_match <- tb_match[!is.na(tb_match$target_name), ]
tb_match
```

Column "score" gives the difference between the query and the target m/z values (in Da) and "ppm_error" the error in ppm.
As you can see, gallic acid was annotated twice, while malvidin-3,5-diglucoside was not detected. The second case was expected, since anthocyanins are positively charged and do not ionize well in negative ion mode. When a compound is annotated more than once, we keep the chromatographic peak with the highest intensity.

```{r}
tb_match <- tb_match[order(tb_match$maxo, decreasing = TRUE), ]
tb_match <- tb_match[!duplicated(tb_match$target_name), ]
```

At this point we can add to our reference database the retention time of each analytical standard:

```{r}
stds_tb$RT <- tb_match$rt[match(stds_tb$name, tb_match$target_name)]
stds_tb
```

Finally, we check if in this injection MS/MS spectra of the standards were recorded:

```{r}
## load the MS/MS data
std_MSMS <- readMsExperiment(spectraFiles = std_files[1]) |>
  filterMsLevel(2)   ## only fragmentation

## create a query data.frame with the precursor m/z and retention time of each MS/MS spectrum
std_MSMS_tb <- data.frame(
  mz = precursorMz(spectra(std_MSMS)),
  rtime = rtime(spectra(std_MSMS))
)

## annotation based on the precursor m/z
MSMS_match <- matchMz(
  std_MSMS_tb, stds_tb, param = MzParam(ppm = 10)
)
MSMS_match
MSMS_match_tb <- matchedData(MSMS_match)
MSMS_match_tb <- MSMS_match_tb[!is.na(MSMS_match_tb$target_name), ]
MSMS_match_tb
```

In this injection MS/MS spectra were recorded for only `r length(unique(MSMS_match_tb$target_name))` of the `r nrow(stds_tb)` analytical standards (`r paste(unique(MSMS_match_tb$target_name), collapse = ", ")`). In DDA the instrument fragments only the most intense ions of each full scan, so the other standards, even when they give a chromatographic peak, were never selected for fragmentation. Let's keep this information: later it will be useful to compare these MS/MS spectra with the ones collected in the wine samples, to confirm their annotation with a higher confidence.


## Annotation of study samples

We are now ready to see if any of the compounds of "mix 2" are present in the study samples.

We load the processed data:

```{r}
load("processed_wines_data.RData")
head(feat)
```

We annotate the features with our reference table, using this time both m/z and retention time, with the functions `matchValues()` and `MzRtParam()`.

```{r}
ft_match <- matchValues(
  feat, stds_tb, param = MzRtParam(ppm = 10, toleranceRt = 5),
  mzColname = c("mzmed", "mz"),
  rtColname = c("rtmed", "RT")
)
ft_match
```

Let's see which compounds were found:

```{r}
ft_tb_match <- matchedData(ft_match)
ft_tb_match <- ft_tb_match[!is.na(ft_tb_match$target_name), ]
ft_tb_match
```

Considering both m/z and retention time, `r nrow(ft_tb_match)` of the `r nrow(stds_tb)` compounds of mix 2 are observed in the wine samples: `r paste(ft_tb_match$target_name, collapse = ", ")`.

Below we plot the feature of gallic acid in the study samples, with a vertical line at the retention time of the analytical standard:

```{r}
gallic_acid <- stds_tb[stds_tb$name == "Gallic acid", ]
ga_feature <- rownames(ft_tb_match)[ft_tb_match$target_name == "Gallic acid"]

ft_chr <- featureChromatograms(raw_data_filled,
                               features = ga_feature,
                               expandRt = 15,
                               filled = FALSE)
sample_colors <- c(red = "#8B3A3A80", wht = "#FFA50080", X = "#80808080")[sampleData(raw_data_filled)$color]
plot(ft_chr, col = sample_colors,
     peakBg = sample_colors[chromPeaks(ft_chr)[, "sample"]])
abline(v = gallic_acid$RT, lwd = 10, col = "#D2D2D290")
```

Finally, let's compare the MS/MS spectrum of gallic acid recorded in the analytical standard with the MS/MS spectra of this feature recorded in the study samples:

```{r}
## the MS/MS spectrum of the standard
ga_MSMS <- std_MSMS |>
  spectra() |>
  filterPrecursorMzValues(gallic_acid$mz, ppm = 10) |>
  filterRt(gallic_acid$RT + 5 * c(-1, 1))

## all the MS/MS spectra in the study samples with the m/z and retention time of gallic acid
MSMS_data <- readMsExperiment(spectraFiles = sampleData(raw_data_filled)$filepath) |>
  filterMsLevel(2)   ## only fragmentation

ga_MSMS_data <- MSMS_data |>
  spectra() |>
  filterPrecursorMzValues(gallic_acid$mz, ppm = 10) |>
  filterRt(gallic_acid$RT + 5 * c(-1, 1))
ga_MSMS_data
```

In the study samples there are `r length(ga_MSMS_data)` MS/MS spectra with precursor m/z and retention time similar to the ones of gallic acid.
Below we compare in a mirror plot the most intense of them (top) with the MS/MS spectrum of the analytical standard (bottom):

```{r}
best_sample <- which.max(precursorIntensity(ga_MSMS_data))

mirror_df <- bind_rows(
  as_tibble(peaksData(ga_MSMS_data)[[best_sample]]) |>
    mutate(spectrum = paste("wine:", basename(dataOrigin(ga_MSMS_data)[best_sample]))),
  as_tibble(peaksData(ga_MSMS)[[1]]) |>
    mutate(spectrum = "standard")
) |>
  mutate(rel_intensity = intensity / max(intensity), .by = spectrum) |>
  mutate(rel_intensity = if_else(spectrum == "standard", -rel_intensity, rel_intensity))

ggplotly(
  mirror_df |>
    ggplot(aes(x = mz, xend = mz, y = 0, yend = rel_intensity, col = spectrum)) +
    geom_segment() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, col = "gray50") +
    scale_color_manual(values = c("#8B3A3A", "gray30"), name = NULL) +
    labs(x = "m/z", y = "relative intensity") +
    theme_light()
)
```


## How similar are the two spectra?

Looking at the mirror plot is useful, but we would like to have a number. The most common measure of similarity between two MS/MS spectra is the *normalized dot product*: the peaks of the two spectra are matched on their m/z values and their intensities are compared. It goes from 0 (nothing in common) to 1 (identical spectra). `compareSpectra()` calculates it for all the pairs of spectra:

```{r}
compareSpectra(ga_MSMS_data, ga_MSMS, ppm = 10, tolerance = 0.005)
```

Mmm ... the base peak (m/z 125.02, gallic acid after the loss of CO~2~) is the same, but the similarity is really low! Let's look at the quality of the spectra. Two simple measures are:

* the **number of peaks**
* the **spectral entropy**: the Shannon entropy of the relative intensities of the peaks. It is 0 for a spectrum with a single peak and it grows when the signal is spread on many peaks of similar intensity ... as it happens with noise

```{r}
spectra_quality <- \(x) tibble(
  file = basename(dataOrigin(x)),
  rt = rtime(x),
  n_peaks = lengths(x),
  base_peak = vapply(intensity(x), max, numeric(1)),
  entropy = entropy(x, normalized = FALSE)
)

spectra_quality(ga_MSMS)
spectra_quality(ga_MSMS_data)
```

More than 100 peaks for a small molecule like gallic acid? The spectra are centroided (the base peak at m/z 125.02 is a single point), but if we zoom on the low m/z region of the spectrum of the standard we see something strange: a band of tens of centroids, a few mDa apart, with irregular intensities

```{r}
peaksData(ga_MSMS)[[1]] |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  subset(mz < 52)
```

These bands are noise: they increase the entropy of the spectra and, since they fall at different m/z in every spectrum, they make the spectra less similar to each other.

## A possible solution

For the last point we put all the steps we did for mix 02 in a function, which builds the library of a mix (m/z and retention time of each standard) ...

```{r}
build_library <- \(mix_file, compounds) {
  lib <- compounds |>
    mutate(mass = calculateMass(formula),
           mz = as.numeric(mass2mz(mass, "[M-H]-")))
  pks <- readMsExperiment(spectraFiles = mix_file) |>
    filterMsLevel(1) |>
    findChromPeaks(param = cwp) |>
    chromPeaks()
  pks_match <- matchedData(matchMz(pks, as.data.frame(lib), param = MzParam(ppm = 10)))
  pks_match <- pks_match[!is.na(pks_match$target_name), ]
  pks_match <- pks_match[order(pks_match$maxo, decreasing = TRUE), ]
  pks_match <- pks_match[!duplicated(pks_match$target_name), ]
  lib |>
    mutate(RT = pks_match$rt[match(name, pks_match$target_name)])
}
```

... and we apply it to mix 04 (no anthocyanins here, so all the compounds are neutral)

```{r}
mix04 <- tibble(
  name = c("Kaempferol-3-glucoside", "p-Coumaric acid", "2,4-Dihydroxybenzoic acid",
           "Caffeic acid ethyl ester", "(-)-Catechin-3-O-gallate", "Epigallocatechin gallate",
           "(-)-Gallocatechin", "Isorhamnetin-3-rutinoside", "Procyanidin B1"),
  formula = c("C21H20O11", "C9H8O3", "C7H6O4", "C11H12O4", "C22H18O10", "C22H18O11",
              "C15H14O7", "C28H32O16", "C30H26O12")
)

mix04_lib <- build_library(list.files("../data/wines/", pattern = "mix04", full.names = TRUE), mix04)
mix04_lib
```

Now we can annotate the features of the wines

```{r}
mix04_match <- matchValues(
  feat, as.data.frame(mix04_lib |> filter(!is.na(RT))),
  param = MzRtParam(ppm = 10, toleranceRt = 5),
  mzColname = c("mzmed", "mz"),
  rtColname = c("rtmed", "RT")
)

mix04_tb <- matchedData(mix04_match)
mix04_tb <- mix04_tb[!is.na(mix04_tb$target_name), ]
mix04_tb[, c("mzmed", "rtmed", "target_name", "target_RT", "ppm_error")]
```

Note that three compounds of mix 04 are isomers of compounds of mix 02: they have the same formula and the same m/z

```{r}
isomers <- inner_join(stds_tb |> select(name, formula, RT),
                      mix04_lib |> select(name, formula, RT),
                      by = "formula", suffix = c("_mix02", "_mix04")) |>
  mutate(delta_RT = abs(RT_mix02 - RT_mix04))
isomers
```

Here m/z alone is not enough, and the retention time has to do the job. It works for the pairs which elute far apart (more than the 5 s tolerance we used for the matching), but `r isomers$name_mix02[which.min(isomers$delta_RT)]` and `r isomers$name_mix04[which.min(isomers$delta_RT)]` elute only `r round(min(isomers$delta_RT), 1)` s apart: a feature at that m/z and retention time could be either of them, and only the MS/MS spectrum could help.
